source_text: Igitur gradum conferamus, et summam quaestionis ipsius certis lineis determinemus. Cur etenim Deus, universitatis conditor, mundi totius gubernator, hominis plasmator, universarum gentium sator, legem per Moysen uni populo dedisse credatur, et non omnibus gentibus attribuisse dicatur? Nisi enim omnibus eam dedisset, nullo pacto ad eam etiam proselytos ex gentibus accessum habere permitteret: sed, ut congruit bonitati Dei et aequitati ipsius, utpote plasmatoris generis humani, omnibus gentibus eamdem legem dedit: quam certis et statutis temporibus observari praecepit, quando voluit, et per quos voluit, et sicut voluit. Namque in principio mundi, ipsi Adae et Evae legem dedit, ne de fructu arboris plantatae in medio paradisi ederent; quod si contra fecissent, morte morerentur: quae lex eis sufficeret, si esset custodita. In hac enim lege Adae data, omnia praecepta condita recognoscimus quae postea pullulaverunt data per Moysen, id est, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum de toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua; et, Diliges proximum tibi tanquam te; et, Non occides, non moechaberis, non furaberis, falsum testimonium non dices. Honora patrem tuum et matrem: et, Alienum non concupisces. Primordialis lex est enim data Adae et Evae in paradiso, quasi matrix omnium praeceptorum Dei. Denique, si Dominum Deum suum dilexissent, contra praeceptum ejus non fecissent: si proximum diligerent, id est semetipsos, persuasioni serpentis non credidissent; atque ita in semetipsos homicidium non commisissent, excidendo de immortalitate, faciendo contra Dei praeceptum; a furto quoque abstinuissent, si de fructu arboris clam non degustassent, nec a conspectu Domini Dei sui sub arbore delitescere gestissent: nec falsum asseveranti diabolo participes efficerentur, credendo ei quod similes Dei essent futuri: atque ita nec Deum offendissent, ut patrem, qui eos de limo terrae quasi ex utero matris figuraverat: si alienum non concupissent, de fructu illicito non gustassent. Igitur in hac generali et primordiali Dei lege, quam in arboris fructu observari Deus sanxerat, omnia praecepta legis posterioris specialiter indita fuisse cognoscimus, quae suis temporibus edita germinaverunt Ejusdem est enim postea subdocere legem, qui ante praemiserat praeceptum, quoniam et ipsius est erudire postea qui ante justos formare instituerat. Quid enim mirum, si is auget disciplinam qui instituit? si is perfecit qui coepit? Denique ante legem Moysi scriptam in tabulis lapideis legem fuisse contendo non scriptam, quae naturaliter intelligebatur, et a patribus custodiebatur. Nam unde Noe justus inventus, si non illum naturalis legis justitia praecedebat? unde Abraham amicus Dei deputatus, si non de aequitate et justitiae legis naturalis? unde Melchisedech sacerdos Dei summi nuncupatus, si non ante Leviticae legis sacerdotium Levitae fuerunt, qui sacrificia Deo offerebant? Sic enim post supra scriptos patriarchas data lex est Moysi eo tempore posteaquam ab Aegypto excesserunt, post intervallum multorum temporum et spatia Denique, post quadringentos et triginta annos Abrahae data est lex. Unde intelligimus Dei legem etiam ante Moysen, nec in Horeb tantum, aut in Sina et in cremo, sed antiquiorem primum in paradiso, post patriarchis, atque ita et Judaeis certis temporibus reformatam; ut non jam ad Moysi legem ita attendamus, quasi ad principalem legem, sed ad subsequentem, quam certo tempore Deus et gentibus exhibuit, et repromissam per prophetas in melius reformavit, et praemonuit futurum ut, sicuti certo tempore data est lex per Moysen, ita temporaliter observata et custodita credatur: nec adimamus hanc Dei potestatem, pro temporum conditione legis praecepta reformantem in hominis salutem. Denique, qui contendit et sabbatum adhuc observandum quasi salutis medelam, circumcisionem octavi diei propter mortis comminationem, doceat in praeteritum justos sabbatizasse aut circumcidisse, et sic amicos Dei effectos. Nam, si circumcisio purgat hominem, Deus Adam incircumcisum cum faceret, cur eum non circumcidit, vel posteaquam deliquit, si purgat circumcisio? Certe in paradiso constituens eum incircumcisum, colonum paradisi praefecit. Igitur, cum neque circumcisum neque sabbatizantem Deus Adam instituerit, consequenter quoque sobolem ejus Abel offerentem sibi sacrificia, incircumcisum nec sabbatizantem laudavit, accepto ferens quae offerebat in simplicitate cordis, et reprobans sacrificium fratris ejus Cain, qui non offerebat, non recte dividebat. Noe quoque incircumcisum Deus, sed et non sabbatizantem, de diluvio liberavit. Nam et Enoch justissimum non circumcisum, nec sabbatizantem, de hoc mundo transtulit; qui necdum mortem gustavit, ut aeternitatis candidatus, jam nobis ostenderet nos quoque sine legis onere Moysi, Deo posse placere. Melchisedech quoque summi Dei sacerdos incircumcisus, et non sabbatizans, ad sacerdotium Dei allectus est. Probat et Loth frater Abrahae, quod pro meritis justitiae suae sine legis observatione de Sodomitarum incendio sit liberatus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, let us compare the step and determine the sum of the question itself with certain lines. For why is God, the founder of the universe, the governor of the whole world, the shaper of man, the sower of all nations, believed to have given the law through Moses to one people, and not to have attributed it to all nations? For if He had not given it to all, He would not have permitted even proselytes from the nations to have access to it. But, as is fitting to the goodness of God and His equity, as the shaper of the human race, He gave the same law to all nations, which He commanded to be observed at certain and established times, when He willed, and through whom He willed, and as He willed. For in the beginning of the world, He gave the law to Adam and Eve themselves, not to eat of the fruit of the tree planted in the middle of paradise, which if they had done against, they would have died by death, a law that would have been sufficient for them if it had been kept. In this law given to Adam, we recognize all the commandments that were later given through Moses, that is, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and You shall love your neighbor as yourself, and You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother, and You shall not covet what belongs to another. The primordial law was given to Adam and Eve in paradise, as the matrix of all God's commandments. Finally, if they had loved the Lord their God, they would not have acted against His commandment, if they had loved their neighbor, that is, themselves, they would not have believed the serpent's persuasion, and thus they would not have committed homicide against themselves, cutting themselves off from immortality, acting against God's commandment, and they would have abstained from theft, if they had not secretly tasted the fruit of the tree, nor would they have hidden from the sight of the Lord their God under the tree. They would not have become participants in the false assertion of the devil, believing him that they would be like God. Thus, they would not have offended God, as their father, who had formed them from the clay of the earth as if from their mother's womb. If they had not coveted what belonged to another, they would not have tasted the forbidden fruit. Therefore, in this general and primordial law of God, which God had sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree, we recognize that all the commandments of the later law were specially given, which were published at their times and germinated. It is the same God who later teaches the law, who previously sent forth the commandment, since it is also His to instruct later those whom He had previously formed as just. What is surprising, if He who instituted increases discipline, if He who began perfects? Finally, I contend that before the written law of Moses on stone tablets, there was an unwritten law, which was naturally understood and kept by the fathers. For whence was Noah found just, if not the justice of the natural law had preceded him? Whence was Abraham called the friend of God, if not from the equity and justice of the natural law? Whence was Melchizedek called the priest of the most high God, if not before the Levitical priesthood, the Levites were, who offered sacrifices to God? Thus, the law was given to Moses at that time, after they had come out of Egypt, after an interval of many times and spaces. Finally, after four hundred and thirty years, the law was given to Abraham. From which we understand that God's law was also before Moses, not only in Horeb, or in Sinai, or in the desert, but earlier, first in paradise, and later to the patriarchs, and thus also to the Jews, at certain times reformed, so that we do not now attend to Moses' law as if it were the primary law, but as a subsequent one, which God exhibited to the nations at a certain time, and which He promised through the prophets to reform for the better, and foretold that it would come to pass, just as the law was given through Moses at a certain time, so it is believed to have been observed and kept temporarily. We do not take away this power of God, who reforms the commandments of the law according to the condition of the times for the salvation of man. Finally, he who contends that the Sabbath is still to be observed as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day because of the threat of death, let him teach that the just in the past observed the Sabbath or were circumcised, and thus became friends of God. For if circumcision purifies man, why did God not circumcise Adam when He made him, or later, after he had sinned, if circumcision purifies? Certainly, God, establishing him as uncircumcised in paradise, made him the colonel of paradise. Therefore, since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or observing the Sabbath, it follows that He also praised his offspring Abel, who offered sacrifices to Him, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, accepting what he offered in simplicity of heart, and rejecting the sacrifice of his brother Cain, who did not offer it rightly. God also freed Noah, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from the flood. For He also translated Enoch, the most just, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from this world, who had not yet tasted death, so that he might show us that we too can please God without the burden of Moses' law. Melchizedek, the priest of the most high God, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, was called to the priesthood of God. Lot, the brother of Abraham, also proves that he was liberated from the burning of Sodom, without observing the law, because of the merits of his justice.
pass_b_english: Let us then take the next step and pin down the whole issue with clear boundaries. Why is God—the founder of the universe, the governor of the whole world, the shaper of man, the sower of all nations—thought to have given the law through Moses to a single people and not to have assigned it to every nation? If he had not given it to all, he would never have allowed proselytes from the nations access to it. But, as fits the goodness and equity of God, the shaper of the human race, he gave the same law to all nations, commanding it to be observed at fixed, appointed times, whenever he willed, through whomever he willed, and in whatever manner he willed. For at the beginning of the world he gave the law to Adam and Eve themselves: they were not to eat from the fruit of the tree planted in the middle of paradise, and if they disobeyed they would die the death (Genesis 2:16-17); that law would have sufficed for them if they had kept it. In this law given to Adam we recognize every commandment that later sprouted through Moses: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 5:6-21; Exodus 20:1-17), “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother,” and “You shall not covet what belongs to another.” The primordial law was given to Adam and Eve in paradise as the matrix of all God’s commandments. Finally, if they had loved the Lord their God they would not have acted against his commandment; if they had loved their neighbor—that is, themselves—they would not have believed the serpent’s persuasion (Genesis 3:1-7), and so would not have committed homicide against themselves by cutting themselves off from immortality through disobedience; they would have abstained from theft if they had not secretly tasted the fruit, nor would they have tried to hide from the sight of the Lord their God under the tree; they would not have become accomplices in the devil’s false claim that they would become like God; and thus they would not have offended God as their Father, who had formed them from the clay of the earth as from a mother’s womb. If they had not coveted what belonged to another, they would not have tasted the forbidden fruit. Therefore, in this general and primordial law of God, which God sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree, we recognize that all the commandments of the later law were specially implanted, published in their own times, and germinated. It is the same God who later teaches the law who previously sent forth the commandment, since it also belongs to him to instruct later those whom he previously formed as just. What is surprising if the one who instituted increases the discipline, if the one who began brings it to perfection? I contend that before the written law of Moses on stone tablets there was an unwritten law, naturally understood and kept by the fathers. Whence was Noah found just (Genesis 6:9), if not because the justice of the natural law had preceded him? Whence was Abraham called the friend of God (Genesis 15:6), if not from the equity and justice of the natural law? Whence was Melchizedek named priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18-20), if not before the Levitical priesthood existed—the Levites who offered sacrifices to God? Thus the law was given to Moses at that time, after they had come out of Egypt, after an interval of many ages and spaces; finally, after four hundred and thirty years, the law was given to Abraham. From this we understand that God’s law existed even before Moses, not only at Horeb or Sinai or in the desert, but earlier—first in paradise, then with the patriarchs, and so also to the Jews at certain times reformed—so that we no longer treat Moses’ law as if it were the primary law, but as a subsequent one, which God exhibited to the nations at a set time, and which he promised through the prophets to reform for the better, and foretold would come to pass: just as the law was given through Moses at a set time, so it is believed to have been observed and kept temporarily. We do not strip God of this power to reform the commandments of the law according to the condition of the times for the salvation of man. Finally, let the one who contends that the Sabbath must still be observed as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day because of the threat of death, teach that the just in the past observed the Sabbath or were circumcised and so became friends of God. For if circumcision purifies a man, why did God not circumcise Adam when he made him, or later after he had sinned, if circumcision purifies? Certainly, by establishing him as uncircumcised in paradise, God appointed him governor of paradise. Therefore, since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or as a Sabbath-observer, it follows that he also praised his offspring Abel, who offered sacrifices to him uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, accepting what he offered in simplicity of heart and rejecting the sacrifice of his brother Cain, who did not offer it rightly. God also freed Noah, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from the flood. For he also translated Enoch, the most just, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from this world—he had not yet tasted death—so that he might show us that we too can please God without the burden of Moses’ law. Melchizedek, the priest of God Most High, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, was called to the priesthood of God. Lot, Abraham’s brother, also proves that he was liberated from the burning of Sodom without observing the law, because of the merits of his justice.
